name: WWO Cruiserweight Championship
epitaph: Created for a division the WWO's own ledger records as thin from the start — one undated first reign credited to "Solid Rock" Rusty Bowman is the belt's whole early history. Its one dated match is its last: "Problem Child" Chris Stringer beat Andrew "Flash" Tucker in the finals of the WWO's own cruiserweight tournament, Atlantic City, 5 May 2001. The ledger's own notes record what happened next in two steps — the belt itself was converted into the Television Championship for a lack of competition in the division, and six weeks later, on 18 June 2001, that Television Championship was converted again into the International People's Title.

name: WWO Extreme Championship
notes: Ledger source: promotions/wwo/archive/title-history-extreme.html. The ledger's own two entries for American Eagle and Christopher Stonebreaker carry a date conflict the source itself never explains — recorded as printed, not resequenced.
epitaph: Formed by merging the ERW Television Title into the WWO's own championship picture once the two promotions came together, and unified away again within a year: the ledger runs Christopher Stonebreaker's own first reign against Derrick Michaels through American Eagle, Jack "Tower of Terror" Harper, "Big Daddy" Justin Fischer, Vader X and "Prime Time" Phill Massacre — vacated once along the way by Fischer's own departure from the federation — before its own notes record it merged into the International People's Championship. The Extreme Title's own life, start to finish, spans less than a year and a half of the fed's own held record.

name: WWO International People's Championship
epitaph: Absorbed the WWO Extreme Championship's own lineage into itself in a title-unifying match, then ran nine more reigns before the federation's first closure: Tyrant, Ultimate Thrasher, Darkness, Night's Harbinger, "Latin Lightning" Al Perez, "Blockbuster" Johnny Detson and "Money Driven" Mike Sebastian each held it in turn. Detson took it from Perez in Atlanta on 22 July 1999 and lost it to Sebastian in Salt Lake City that November — the ledger's own last recorded change before the belt goes dark for the mid-era gap. Along the way it was held up once after "Prime Time" Phill Massacre was fired from the federation, and Ultimate Thrasher's own reign ended not in a loss but in his failure to appear and defend it. The revived WWO revived the belt itself sideways rather than head-on: its own Cruiserweight Championship, reintroduced by tournament in May 2001, was converted into this title on 18 June 2001 with "Problem Child" Chris Stringer's own cruiserweight reign carrying over — Stringer is still defending it, by countout over Ultimate Thrasher, at the 24 August 2001 Superstar Showcase.

name: WWO International People's Tag Team Titles
notes: Ledger source: promotions/wwo/archive/title-history-ip-tag-team.html. Every reign but the belt's own origin is undated in the source; each is still its own reigns.json row, dated "unknown" per the museum's own honest-gap convention.
epitaph: Won first by Rocky Johnson and Rusty Bowman in a battle royal, the WWO's own International People's Tag Team Titles passed from Continental Connection through the World Leaders, the Bionic Team and Thunderbolts — vacated once when Thunderbolts lost a member to a departure from the federation and sat on hiatus — before Uncivil Disobedience simply stole the belts and declared themselves champions. The ledger's own last word on them: the federation closed with Precious Moments recognized as its final holders.

name: WWO Six-Man Tag Team Title
notes: Ledger source: promotions/wwo/archive/title-history-six-man-tag.html. Every reign but Fire and Ice's own is undated in the source; each is still its own reigns.json row, dated "unknown" per the museum's own honest-gap convention.
epitaph: A short-lived belt: the Lords of the Ring's own undated first reign gave way to Fire and Ice on 23 June 1997, then Aristocracy that July, then Hell's Gate that November — three title changes inside five months. The ledger's own notes say the title was retired outright once Hell's Gate left the WWO, and nothing in the held record revives it.

name: WWO Television Championship
epitaph: Absorbed the WWO Cruiserweight Championship's own lineage in 1999, then changed hands five times in ten months: "Money Driven" Mike Sebastian took it from Night Stalker in Manchester, Apex took it from Sebastian in Orlando, Latex Lex took it from Apex in Roanoke, Dark Soul took it from Lex in Huntington, and "Smooth as Silk" Miguel Quesada took it from Dark Soul in Salt Lake City on 25 November 1999 — the same night, by the ledger's own dating, the International People's Championship also changed hands. The belt's own earlier history records a Lancaster Bomber reign ended by his own firing and a Wuzho reign forfeited when its holder was arrested in Mexico. Quesada is the ledger's own last word: the federation closed with him still champion.

name: WWO Title of the Americas
epitaph: A newly created title with exactly one recorded holder: Papa Legba eliminated Steve Dumars from the ring to win it in Washington, D.C. on 18 June 2001, and the ledger's own "Quick Facts" table still had him champion as of its own 1 December 2001 count, 166 days into the only reign this belt is known to have had.

name: WWO United States Championship
epitaph: Ran through a tournament final to crown its first champion, The Heckler, and passed through King $$$ Perfect and Andros before Lord Keeblor won it from "Prime Time" Michael Fulton in Auckland on 1 October 1997 — the first of two reigns the ledger credits him with. Underground Kingpin's own two reigns bracket a CJ Gesner title win in between, and "The Prodigy" Tracy Hudson took the belt from "Money Driven" Mike Sebastian in Atlanta on 22 July 1999 before losing it back in the same city, to Lord Keeblor a second time, on 17 March 2000. The ledger's own notes record the federation closing on that same day.

name: WWO World Title
epitaph: The WWO's top belt, run through a tournament to crown King $$$ Perfect after its own earliest history and on through Tony Tobis, "Ravashing" Ric Studd and "The Master and Ruler of the World" before Randy Bryson won a tournament final on 1 May 1997 after the previous champion's retirement. Andros, Zac Schneider, Iron, Bellamy and Lord Robert d'Artois traded it through 1997 and 1998 — Bellamy's own reign ending in a cage match billed as the Valentine's Day Massacre — before Fury took it and held it 369 days, the longest total reign the ledger's own "Quick Facts" table records, ending only when Fury was forced to retire from professional wrestling. Ultimate Thrasher and a wrestler billed as Roundhouse then traded it five times across 1999 alone, before "Mr. Ratings" Warren Hayes took it in a battle royal on 15 January 2000, knocking out Mike Sebastian to end it — the ledger's own last recorded champion. The held record then goes dark: by the time the revived WWO's Superstar Showcase resumes coverage on 24 August 2001, Tyrone "Purple" Hayes is already champion, defending against Steve Dumars, and nothing the museum holds explains how the belt passed from Warren Hayes to him.

name: WWO World Tag Team Titles
epitaph: The WWO's own busiest championship by the ledger's own count — the Business Men, World Leaders, Lethal Weapons and Mean Mason/DOC traded it four times inside eleven days in December 1997 alone, and World Leaders' own three total reigns lead every team the ledger names. Uncivil Disobedience won it from Don't You Wish You Were Us in Los Angeles on 21 October 1998, and by 2001 the belts had passed to Physicians Advocating Innovative Neoprocedures, who took them from Vegas Connection in Washington, D.C. on 18 June 2001 and lost them back to the same team in Milwaukee just six weeks later, on 29 July 2001 — the ledger's own last recorded change. The federation's own notes name Thunderstorm, an earlier holder, as "the final WWO tag team champions of 2000," leaving the 2001 Vegas Connection/P.A.I.N. exchanges as a coda the notes themselves never reconcile against that claim.

name: WWO European Commonwealth Championship
notes: First recognised on the WWO's Spotlight broadcast of 27 April 2002 in San Francisco.
epitaph: Recognised by the WWO's president on the Spotlight of 27 April 2002 with Nathaniel Knowitall as its champion and a title defence ordered for the same night. Matt Cole won it from him there, then threw the belt into the crowd. Two reigns on record, both begun that night.
